title: XSS Defence: Encoding, CSP and Safe Frameworks
summary: Quick revision notes on stored, reflected and DOM XSS, and the layers that stop them: context-aware output encoding, Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies, and framework auto-escaping with its escape hatches.

chapters.title: XSS Mental Model: Stored, Reflected, DOM
points: XSS = attacker-controlled data is interpreted as code in the victim's browser, running with the page's origin and so able to read the DOM, make same-origin requests and act as the user
Stored XSS: payload is saved server-side (comment, profile name) and served to every viewer; highest impact because no crafted link is needed
Reflected XSS: payload sits in the request (query string, form field) and is echoed in that one response; needs the victim to click a crafted URL

DOM XSS: client JS moves a source (location.hash, location.search, document.referrer, postMessage) into a sink (innerHTML, document.write, eval, setTimeout(string), element.href) and the server may never see the payload (always true for location.hash and postMessage; location.search is still sent to the server)
Interview Point: (1) Which XSS type never reaches the server and how do you find it? (2) Why is stored XSS worse than reflected? (3) Name two DOM sources and two sinks.

chapters.title: Context-Aware Output Encoding
points: Core rule: encode on output, for the exact context where the data lands; validating input is defence in depth, not the fix
HTML body: encode < > & " ' to entities (< > & " ')
HTML attribute: always quote the attribute value and encode quotes; unquoted attributes can be broken out of with a space (x onmouseover=alert(1))

JavaScript, URL and CSS contexts each need their own encoder: JS string uses \xHH escapes or JSON.stringify inside a data attribute; URL parameter uses encodeURIComponent; URL scheme must be allowlisted (http/https), never javascript:

Interview Point: (1) Why does HTML-encoding not protect a value placed inside a <script> block or an href? (2) Encode on input or on output, and why? (3) How do you safely pass server data to client JS?

chapters.title: CSP and HttpOnly Cookies as Containment
points: CSP is a response header listing allowed script sources; it is a second layer that limits damage when an escaping bug slips through, not a replacement for encoding
Strong policy: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'nonce-R4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'. The nonce must be fresh per response and unguessable

'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' or wildcard hosts (https:, *.cdn.com) in script-src largely cancel CSP's protection; inline event handlers are blocked unless allowed. Roll out first with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only plus report-to
HttpOnly cookie hides the session cookie from document.cookie, so XSS cannot steal it; add Secure and SameSite=Lax/Strict. It does NOT stop XSS from sending authenticated requests as the user
Interview Point: (1) What does HttpOnly protect and what does it not? (2) Why is a nonce-based CSP stronger than a host allowlist? (3) How do you deploy CSP without breaking the site?

chapters.title: Framework Auto-Escaping and Its Escape Hatches
points: React JSX, Angular templates, Vue mustaches and Django/Rails templates (and Jinja2 when autoescape is enabled, as Flask does for .html) escape interpolated text by default, which makes the safe path the easy path

Escape hatches turn escaping off: React dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue v-html, Angular bypassSecurityTrustHtml and [innerHTML] with a bypass, Jinja |safe and autoescape off, Django mark_safe, Rails raw and html_safe
If raw HTML is unavoidable, sanitise with an allowlist sanitiser such as DOMPurify (client) or a server-side equivalent immediately before rendering, and never write your own regex filter

Auto-escaping only covers text positions: user-controlled href/src (javascript: URLs), style, event-handler attributes, server-side template injection and direct DOM writes (ref.innerHTML) stay unprotected

Interview Point: (1) Name three escape hatches and the safe alternative for each. (2) Why is <a href={userUrl}> risky in React 18 and earlier (React 19 blocks javascript: URLs), and why still allowlist URL schemes? (3) When is a sanitiser needed instead of encoding?

chapters.title: Common XSS Mistakes
points: Blacklist filtering (strip
Encoding for the wrong context, e.g. HTML-escaping a value then inserting it into a JS string, an unquoted attribute or a URL
Using innerHTML or document.write for plain text; use textContent or innerText, which never parse markup
Trusting HttpOnly or CSP alone, and keeping 'unsafe-inline' in script-src without a nonce or hash, so injected inline script runs
Interview Point: (1) Why does a blacklist fail? (2) What is the one-line fix for innerHTML with user text? (3) Which mistake makes a CSP useless?

chapters.title: XSS Defence Cheat Sheet
points: Types: stored (saved, hits all viewers) / reflected (in the request, needs a link) / DOM (client source to sink, server often blind, e.g. #fragment)
Encode by context: HTML body entities, quoted attributes, JS \xHH or JSON, URL encodeURIComponent plus scheme allowlist
Defence layers in order: auto-escaping templates, then allowlist sanitiser for rich HTML, then nonce + strict-dynamic CSP, then HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies
Grep for sinks in review: innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, eval, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, |safe, mark_safe, bypassSecurityTrust*
Interview Point: (1) Walk through your defence layers for a comment box. (2) What does each layer stop and miss? (3) How would you audit an existing app for XSS?
